Creating successful preventative and intervention plans requires an understanding of the many, multi-level factors that contribute to psychological discomfort. The objective of this scoping review was to use the Socio-Ecological Model (SEM) to map the determinants of psychological distress among college students in a comprehensive manner. Methods: A total of 15 review publi- cations published between 2015 and 2024, including narrative reviews, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and umbrella reviews, were analyzed under the guidance of PRISMA ScR. These studies synthesized evidence across various countries, including China, Iran, India, Canada, Egypt, Nigeria, Saudi Arabia, and the United States. Results: Academic pressure, financial stress, poor sleep, unhealthy coping mechanisms, and pre-existing mental health issues were all individual-level concerns, with female and minority students being more vulnerable. Strong familial ties and friendships served as protective interpersonal support. Heavy academic workloads, strict grading guidelines, a lack of mental health resources, and unwelcoming campus environments were among the institutional factors. Stigma and socioeconomic disparities are examples of community-level variables that make mental health issues worse. Conclusions: Student mental health is shaped by interrelated factors across all SEM levels. Integrated, multi-level strategies are essential to fostering supportive campuses, strengthening community networks, and implementing inclusive policies that promote mental health equity. Mental health problems among college students have consistently increased over time and it poses a threat to their health and academic performance (Lipson, Lattie, & Eisenberg, 2019). Identification of mental health disorders among college students have been overlooked. Depression is the second most common mental health disorder among college students in the United States (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students are a key population for determining the economic growth and success of the nation. Thus, primary healthcare providers are the front line to early screening and identification of depression amongst college students. Problem Statement The prevalence of depression has risen in the college population in the past decade. There is an estimation of 33.3% of college students exhibiting significant symptoms of depression, generalized anxiety disorder, or suicide ideation (Oswalt et al., 2018). Depression is one of the most common mental health conditions among college students. In the United States, approximately 26% of individuals ages 18 and older live with a diagnosable mental health disorder in a given year (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students with depression can experience a decrease in physical health, negatively impact mental health, hinder relationships, impede academic endeavors, and decrease quality of life (Pedrelli, Nyer, Yeung, Zulauf, & Wilens, 2015). Local Problem An identified public college health center had a complaint-based approach to depression screening. A complaint-based approach screens for depression if a patient presented with depression-related symptoms. Patients may mask their depressive symptoms and suicidal intent by complaining of other health issues. Patients may report somatic symptoms in an attempt to avoid mental health stigma. Thus, the complaint-based approach may under-detect and under- treat depression. The Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) could be utilized as a first step approach to screen college students for depression during every visit at the college health center. The PHQ-2 has two questions and can easily be administered by healthcare providers at the college health center. College students who screen positive should be further evaluated with the PHQ-9 and possibly referred to counseling services at the identified public college. The counseling center at the identified public college provides an array of mental health services that could be beneficial for college students who are experiencing depression, but college students should first be screened and identified.
